<reason>B anchored the entire debate on the motion's operative word "over" and made it stick: everything agreeable in A's plan (processing, manufacturing) needed no prioritization trade-off, while everything that actually deprioritized rich-market exports (the levy, diverted corridors, the regional tariff wall) carried costs A never cleanly absorbed. B turned both of A's marquee examples — Korea sold ships and chips to America, Indonesia's smelters served Chinese demand — and A's challenge for a precedent of industrialization by deprioritizing rich markets went unanswered all debate. The levy dilemma (a tax that bites costs the foreign exchange that funds industrialization; one that doesn't is no priority) was only dissolved by A in the closing, too late and too thinly. A fought well: the import-demand argument, concrete policy answers under pressure, and a sharp "your position opposes nothing" closing frame kept this competitive, and B's clipped Rebuttal 2 plus occasional overreach in defending dig-and-ship Australia cost B some ground. But B made the decision rule clearer, answered pressure more directly, and left A's central burdens standing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1: seizing A's own line that "the destination of the cargo is a detail" to argue half the motion had been conceded, then flipping the Indonesia nickel example (Chinese capital, Chinese battery demand) so A's best evidence became B's — A never fully recovered from that double turn.</best_rebuttal>
